title: Alentejo
description: Southern Portugal's hot plains: ripe, generous reds, cork forests and the Roman clay pots called talhas.
L: Alentejo means beyond the Tagus, the river south of Lisbon. It covers about a third of Portugal, mostly rolling plains with cork oak and olive groves, and some hills like the São Mamede range near Portalegre. It has about 23,000 hectares of vines. Portugal produces about half the world's cork, much of it here.

The climate is Mediterranean with continental influence: very hot, dry summers, often over 40 degrees, and mild winters. Rainfall is low. Irrigation is common, especially from the Alqueva reservoir, Europe's largest artificial lake, completed in 2002. Higher sites, like Portalegre, are cooler and fresher.
The region lies beyond, south of, the Tagus river.

The Alentejo DOC has eight sub-regions, including Reguengos, Borba, Redondo, Vidigueira and Portalegre. Vidigueira, sheltered by a fault escarpment, is known for whites; Portalegre, at up to 900 m, for fresh wines from old field blends. Much wine is sold as Vinho Regional Alentejano, with more flexible rules.
Portalegre is one of the Alentejo's cooler sub-regions.
Yes. Altitude in the São Mamede hills keeps it fresh.

Explain the role of Alicante Bouschet

Aragonez, Tempranillo, gives red fruit and body. Trincadeira gives spice, herbs and freshness, but is sensitive to rot. Alicante Bouschet, a French red-fleshed grape, called a teinturier, gives deep colour and structure; it found its best home here. Castelão, Syrah and Touriga Nacional are also common. Reds are ripe, round and generous.

Antão Vaz, from Vidigueira, is the main white: ripe tropical fruit and body, tolerant of heat. Arinto adds acidity; Roupeiro adds aroma. Blends of the three are common. White wines are a growing share, especially from cooler sites.

Alicante Bouschet is one of the few grapes with red flesh. That's why wines from it are so deeply coloured.

Talhas are large clay pots, some holding over 1,000 litres, used in the Alentejo since Roman times. Wine was fermented and stored in them, especially around Vidigueira, Cuba and Vila de Frades. The tradition survived in family cellars, adegas, even as modern wineries took over.

Crushed grapes, with skins and sometimes stems, ferment in the talha. The inside is coated with pez, a resin mixture, to seal it. Skins sink to the bottom and act as a natural filter. The wine stays on its skins until about St Martin's Day, November 11, when talhas are traditionally opened and the wine is drawn from a tap at the base.
Fermented on skins, opened in November
St Martin's Day marks the opening of the new talha wine.

In 2010, the Alentejo DOC created the category DOC Alentejo Vinho de Talha for wines made this way, fermented and stored in clay until at least November 11. Whites, reds, orange wines and rosés can all be made. The style links to the global interest in amphora and skin-contact wines, like Georgia's qvevri.

Reading the Alentejo and eating with it

Labels show Alentejo DOC, sometimes a sub-region like Reguengos or Portalegre, or Vinho Regional Alentejano. Reserva in Portugal means higher alcohol and approval by a tasting panel; Garrafeira means longer ageing. Vinho de Talha marks clay-pot wines. Blends are common; grapes may be listed on the back.

Alentejo food is rustic: black pork, porco preto, from acorn-fed pigs; lamb; migas, bread with pork; açorda, bread soup; and sheep's cheese like Serpa. Reds suit pork and lamb; Antão Vaz whites suit bacalhau and grilled fish. Serve reds at 16 to 18, slightly cool in summer.
